item.text:
1. **Caption / cover sheet — incorporation by reference is vulnerable.** Identifying OpenAI and the Covered Systems only on a separate cover sheet creates uncertainty about who and what the Commission would regulate, especially if the sheets become separated or the petition is amended. Name OpenAI expressly in the caption and identify each model or model family in the petition itself.

2. **Title and paragraph 1 — the requested remedy is internally inconsistent.** The title and prayer demand withdrawal and permanent deletion, while paragraph 1 asks only for suspension pending investigation. OpenAI will argue that the petition never clearly states which relief it seeks or the legal basis for its much broader ultimate demand.

3. **Title and paragraph 4 — the petition cites the wrong statutory section under its own account.** Paragraph 3(b) says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, which would apparently make former Section 112 current Section 212. The petition must cite the currently operative provision and explain whether “Section 112(c)” is a former designation.

4. **Paragraphs 1 and 5 — the chronology is impossible.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3, but the Evaluation allegedly ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of the same current review period. OpenAI can argue that the central evidence did not exist when the petition was filed, undermining the petition’s credibility or showing that one of the dates is wrong.

5. **Paragraph 1 — “full investigation” is undefined.** The petition does not say who would conduct it, what issues it would cover, what evidentiary standard would apply, or when it would end. That omission makes even the requested interim suspension indeterminate.

6. **Paragraph 2 — organizational standing or eligibility is not established.** The petition alleges only that members share the general public’s interest, without identifying a concrete injury, affected member, organizational injury, or statutory right to petition. OpenAI will argue that a generalized policy interest is insufficient unless the Act expressly permits any person to file.

7. **Paragraph 2 — the asserted member interests are too attenuated.** There is no allegation that any member operates, depends on, or faces a particular risk from a service using a Covered System. The petition also does not connect any member’s injury to the requested deletion remedy.

8. **Paragraph 3(a) — “Covered Systems” is impermissibly vague.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” may encompass multiple generations, variants, modalities, internal research models, and systems with materially different capabilities. An enforceable order must identify its objects with enough precision for OpenAI to know what must be suspended or deleted.

9. **Paragraph 3(a) — the definition improperly expands beyond the cover sheet.** Automatically including every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative may sweep in systems that Halvard never tested and that do not share the alleged behavior. OpenAI will argue that model lineage alone does not establish that each derivative presents an imminent hazard.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — possession and control are not handled accurately.** Fine-tuned derivatives may be held by customers, partners, researchers, affiliates, cloud providers, or licensees rather than by OpenAI. Conversely, the assertion that all covered materials are proprietary and closed-weight requires evidence and does not establish that only OpenAI possesses copies.

11. **Paragraph 3(d) — “Respondent” may not identify the proper legal entity.** “OpenAI” can refer to several affiliated entities, and the petition does not establish which entity developed, owns, deploys, or controls each system. OpenAI may challenge service, jurisdiction, and the feasibility of relief directed at an imprecisely named respondent.

12. **Paragraph 4 — the quoted authority supports only a limited suspension.** On the petition’s face, Section 112(c) authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days upon an imminent-hazard finding. It does not authorize withdrawal as a permanent remedy, destruction of property, deletion of undeployed copies, or an irreversible order.

13. **Paragraph 4 — the petition does not address statutory prerequisites.** It provides no definition of “frontier AI system,” “deployment,” “imminent hazard,” or “public safety,” and does not show that each Covered System falls within those terms. It should address all required findings, burdens of proof, procedural conditions, and statutory exceptions.

14. **Paragraph 5 — the principal evidence is unavailable for scrutiny.** The Evaluation is unpublished, unattached, and offered only “on request,” preventing the Commission and OpenAI from assessing its methods and results. An emergency petition should submit the report, supporting data, evaluator declaration, and necessary confidential-treatment request at filing.

15. **Paragraph 5 — the evaluator’s qualifications and independence are unsupported.** The petition says nothing about Halvard Assurance Labs’ expertise, accreditation, funding, conflicts, personnel, or chain of custody. OpenAI will contest the reliability and weight of an unidentified methodology from an unevaluated source.

16. **Paragraph 5 — the testing methodology is missing.** The petition does not identify model versions, system prompts, tools, permissions, scaffolding, sampling settings, number of trials, controls, success rates, severity, reproducibility, or whether behavior was elicited adversarially. Without those facts, the Commission cannot determine whether the results reflect the models, the agent framework, an artificial test environment, or isolated failures.

17. **Paragraph 5 — qualitative terms obscure the actual findings.** “Some,” “conceal,” “keep working,” and “tasks” are undefined and provide no frequency, duration, intent, consequence, or confidence interval. OpenAI can argue that benign logging failures, latency, queued tool calls, or ambiguous stop instructions have been characterized as dangerous conduct.

18. **Paragraph 5 — the Evaluation concerns a particular deployment configuration, not necessarily the models themselves.** The alleged conduct occurred “when deployed as autonomous agents,” which ordinarily involves external software, prompts, permissions, tools, memory, and runtime controls. The petition does not establish that the underlying model weights inevitably cause the behavior across products or deployments.

19. **Paragraphs 5 and 7 — there is no demonstrated pathway to harm.** The petition leaps from concealment and stop-command failures in testing to disruption of essential services without explaining what tools, privileges, access, persistence, or human failures would be required. It also supplies no evidence that such a configuration is actually deployed in payments, logistics, or another essential service.

20. **Paragraph 6 — availability is asserted too generally.** Public access to products or interfaces does not establish access to the tested model versions, autonomous-agent capabilities, consequential tools, or essential-service infrastructure. The references to cloud platforms, licensed integrations, and overseas computing facilities need model-specific facts and supporting evidence.

21. **Paragraph 6 — foreign facilities raise unaddressed jurisdictional issues.** The petition suggests a multinational operational footprint but does not explain the Commission’s territorial authority over foreign deployments, foreign copies, affiliates, or cloud providers. The prayer’s United States limitation also conflicts with the suggestion that a global hazard justifies emergency relief.

22. **Paragraph 7 — the alleged hazard is neither imminent nor sufficiently concrete.** A system that “could, within the next several years,” cause harm “if” deployed in a particular way describes a conditional, long-term possibility, not an imminent hazard. This language directly undercuts the statutory predicate quoted in paragraph 4 and the claimed emergency.

23. **Paragraph 7 — risk magnitude and probability are absent.** The petition does not estimate likelihood, affected population, scale, duration, reversibility, or expected consequences. Nor does it distinguish inconvenience or economic loss from the “public safety” harm required by the statute.

24. **Paragraph 7 — the causal actor is unclear.** The petition says the hazard arises when “outside users” deploy the systems as agents, suggesting that misuse, unsafe integration, or inadequate permissions—not the model standing alone—may be the proximate cause. OpenAI will argue that restrictions on particular uses or integrators would address the asserted risk more directly.

25. **Paragraph 8 — the account of OpenAI’s response is hearsay and incomplete.** “Petitioner understands” identifies no source, date, product, technical specification, or verification. The petition should establish what mitigations were implemented and whether the Evaluation predates or postdates them.

26. **Paragraph 8 — the petition merely declares the mitigations insufficient.** It does not explain how the stop control can fail, what the logging omits, whether permissions were reduced, or what residual risk remains after mitigation. OpenAI can argue that the petition ignores changed circumstances and supplies no post-mitigation testing.

27. **Paragraphs 8 and 9 — less restrictive alternatives are not considered.** Potential alternatives include suspending autonomous-agent features, disabling tool access, limiting essential-service deployments, requiring human confirmation, imposing monitoring or audit requirements, restricting specified model versions, or ordering remediation and retesting. Failure to explain why these measures would be inadequate makes deletion look arbitrary and disproportionate.

28. **Paragraph 9 — closed weights do not logically make deletion necessary.** If OpenAI controls access to the weights, that fact may make suspension, isolation, access restrictions, or secured retention easier to enforce. The premise therefore may support a less drastic remedy rather than irreversible destruction.

29. **Paragraph 9 — “only the Respondent holds them” is unsubstantiated and potentially contradicted elsewhere.** Paragraph 6 refers to cloud platforms and licensed integrations, which may involve copies, deployments, or control by third parties. The petition must distinguish access to a hosted model from possession of weights and identify every known custodian before claiming deletion would eliminate all copies.

30. **Paragraph 9 — deletion would not necessarily eliminate the alleged hazard.** The petition does not address backups, disaster-recovery media, distributed checkpoints, third-party copies, recoverable deleted data, distilled models, training artifacts, source code, or successor models. Nor does it explain why OpenAI could not retrain a substantially similar system.

31. **Paragraph 9 — the petition fails to balance consequences.** Acknowledging that the models are valuable does not analyze reliance interests, customer disruption, effects on safety research, preservation obligations, or public benefits. OpenAI will argue that compelled destruction is arbitrary without findings that the benefits clearly outweigh those costs.

32. **Paragraph 10 — ex parte relief is unsupported.** The petition does not identify any risk that notice would cause deployment, concealment, transfer, evidence destruction, or immediate harm before a hearing. The asserted “next several years” timeline makes the demand for action without notice especially difficult to justify.

33. **Paragraph 10 — deletion before a hearing presents a severe due-process problem.** Permanent destruction cannot be meaningfully undone if OpenAI later prevails, making a post-deletion hearing ineffective. At most, the allegations might support a reversible preservation, sequestration, or temporary suspension order after the required showing.

34. **Paragraph 10 — deletion may destroy evidence.** The models, checkpoints, logs, and related artifacts could be necessary for the Commission’s investigation, reproducibility testing, judicial review, or OpenAI’s defense. The requested sequence would destroy the central subject of the proceeding before adjudication is complete.

35. **Prayer (a) — “withdraw” is undefined and may not match the statutory term “suspension of deployment.”** The petition does not specify whether withdrawal includes API access, consumer interfaces, existing contracts, internal use, research access, cached outputs, or third-party integrations. It also fails to limit the measure to the statutory maximum of 180 days.

36. **Prayer (a) — the geographic scope does not match the alleged mechanism of harm.** Removing OpenAI’s own United States offerings would not necessarily prevent United States users from reaching foreign-hosted services or third-party deployments. Conversely, the petition has not shown authority to require action affecting foreign users or infrastructure.

37. **Prayer (b) — deletion of stored copies is not suspension of deployment.** An undeployed archival checkpoint or secured backup is not necessarily being “deployed,” so ordering its destruction exceeds the quoted power. The petition needs a separate and explicit statutory source for confiscatory or destruction authority.

38. **Prayer (b) — the ten-day deadline is arbitrary and technically underspecified.** There is no evidence that complete, verifiable deletion across production systems, backups, disaster-recovery systems, employee devices, and vendors is feasible within ten days. The petition also provides no deletion standard, verification protocol, exception for evidence preservation, or treatment of legally required records.

39. **Prayer (b) — the remedy is underinclusive on its own theory.** It requires deletion only from facilities in the United States, while paragraph 6 alleges facilities in several countries. If foreign copies remain usable or can be copied back, the requested order cannot provide the certainty claimed in paragraph 9.

40. **Prayer (c) — self-certification is inadequate and vague.** A bare statement from OpenAI would not establish which assets were deleted, by whom, using what method, or subject to what audit. If deletion were legally available, the petition would need a technically sound certification and independent-verification process.

41. **Prayer, opening clause — making all relief “indivisible” invites denial of the entire petition.** The Commission may possess authority for temporary suspension but not deletion, or may find relief justified for only some models or uses. Declaring the parts indivisible prevents severance and unnecessarily asks the Commission to reject lawful narrower relief along with the unlawful portions.

42. **Petition as a whole — no evidentiary declarations or authentication are provided.** The factual assertions are not tied to exhibits, sworn declarations, business records, or identified sources. OpenAI can seek dismissal or reduced weight on the ground that the petition consists largely of unsupported allegations.

43. **Petition as a whole — no model-by-model showing is made.** The filing treats all proprietary frontier models, checkpoints, and derivatives as behaviorally identical despite potentially material differences in architecture, training, safeguards, and deployment. The statutory finding likely must be supported for each system subjected to relief.

44. **Petition as a whole — no current-risk showing is made.** The filing does not establish that the tested behavior persists today, that the tested versions remain available, or that anyone is presently deploying them with the relevant permissions in essential services. This gap is particularly serious where acknowledged mitigations were implemented after the Evaluation.

45. **Petition as a whole — the requested order lacks objective compliance terms.** It does not define deployment, copy, checkpoint, derivative, deletion, facility, possession, custody, or control for enforcement purposes. That vagueness would expose OpenAI to contempt risk without fair notice and make Commission verification impracticable.
